questions.stem: Why did the idea of a data warehouse emerge?
options: Because OLTP systems could not store structured data
Because transactional systems were never designed for heavy reporting or analytical workloads
Because businesses wanted to delete historical records
Because relational databases were being replaced by NoSQL
Because cloud storage became free
questions.explanation: OLTP systems record day-to-day operations well but were never designed for heavy reporting, so a centralised analytical datastore was introduced to relieve them and provide trusted historical insight.

questions.stem: What is the distinction between a data warehouse and dimensional modelling?
options: They are two names for the same thing
A data warehouse is a technique; dimensional modelling is a repository
A data warehouse is the central repository consolidating data from many sources, while dimensional modelling is one possible technique for structuring it
Dimensional modelling is used only in OLTP, never in a warehouse
A data warehouse must always use dimensional modelling
questions.explanation: The warehouse is the central repository; dimensional modelling is only one of several techniques (with 3NF and ensemble approaches) for structuring that repository.

questions.stem: Which data warehouse modelling approach, popularised by Bill Inmon, emphasises integration and normalisation to minimise redundancy?
options: Star schema
Third Normal Form (3NF)
Data Vault
OLAP cube
Galaxy schema
questions.explanation: The 3NF approach, popularised by Bill Inmon, aims to minimise redundancy and create a subject-oriented, integrated structure, though it can be complex for end-user queries.

questions.stem: In dimensional modelling, what does a fact table keep?
options: The data points by which analysis is sliced, such as time or region
The transaction's lowest level of data, numeric or non-numeric, such as sales numbers or clicks
The metadata describing each source system
Hubs, links and satellites
Pre-aggregated multidimensional totals
questions.explanation: A fact table keeps the transaction's lowest level of data, which can be numeric or non-numeric, such as sales numbers, clicks on a social media portal or searches in Google.

options: A dimension that has been normalised into related tables
A dimension that can connect to multiple facts
A dimension stored in a data mart only
A dimension that never changes
A dimension holding only numeric values
questions.explanation: A conformed dimension is a dimension which can connect to multiple fact tables.

questions.stem: Which modelling approach structures data into hubs, links and satellites to support historical tracking and auditability?
options: Snowflake schema
Anchor modelling
Data Vault
Hook model
Third Normal Form
questions.explanation: Data Vault, one of the ensemble modelling approaches, structures data into hubs, links and satellites to support historical tracking and auditability.

questions.stem: What is the main difference between a data warehouse and a data mart?
options: A warehouse uses dimensional modelling while a mart uses 3NF
A warehouse allows deletions while a mart does not
A warehouse consolidates data at enterprise level, while a mart is scoped to a department or function such as Finance or Sales
A warehouse is virtual while a mart is physical
A warehouse stores raw data while a mart stores only cubes
questions.explanation: Both share the same design principles and may use any modelling technique; the difference is scale and focus, with warehouses serving the whole organisation and marts delivering subject-specific solutions.

questions.stem: How did Bill Inmon define a data warehouse in 1990?
options: A copy of transaction data specifically structured for query and analysis
A subject-oriented, integrated, time-variant and non-volatile collection of data in support of management's decision-making process
A centralised repository of raw data in any format
A set of hubs, links and satellites
A virtual layer over distributed sources
questions.explanation: Inmon, regarded as the Father of Data Warehousing, defined it as a subject-oriented, integrated, time-variant and non-volatile collection of data supporting management decision-making.

questions.stem: How do the approaches of Bill Inmon and Ralph Kimball differ in building order?
options: Inmon builds marts first (bottom-up); Kimball builds the enterprise warehouse first (top-down)
Inmon builds the enterprise warehouse first (top-down); Kimball starts with business-driven data marts (bottom-up)
Both build marts first but differ on schema type
Both build the warehouse first but Kimball uses 3NF
Inmon rejects data marts entirely
questions.explanation: Inmon's top-down method builds the enterprise warehouse (typically 3NF) first and then populates dependent marts; Kimball's bottom-up approach starts with data marts that are later integrated.

questions.stem: Why does the author of I Am Datapedia! prefer building the enterprise warehouse before the data marts?
options: Because marts cannot use dimensional modelling
Because regulators require a warehouse first
Because if marts are built first, any change at warehouse level forces modifications in marts and upstream pipelines, adding maintenance overhead
Because warehouses are cheaper to store than marts
Because Kimball recommended it
questions.explanation: Building the warehouse as a foundation and designing marts as tailored subsets gives consistency without redundant effort, avoiding the maintenance overhead of changing marts and pipelines whenever the warehouse changes.
